summary: A VLAN divides one physical switch network into separate logical Layer 2 broadcast domains. IEEE 802.1Q tags frames with a VLAN ID so many VLANs can share one trunk link.

sections.heading: Why VLANs
bullets: Segment traffic by department, function, or security zone without separate hardware.
Each VLAN is typically one IP subnet.

sections.heading: The 802.1Q tag
sections.body: A 4-byte tag is inserted after the source MAC address:
bullets: VID: VLAN ID; usable values 1-4094 (0 and 4095 are reserved).
The tag adds 4 bytes, raising the maximum frame to 1522; the FCS is recalculated.
sections.code: | Dst MAC | Src MAC | TPID 0x8100 (16) | PCP (3) | DEI (1) | VID (12) | EtherType | Payload | FCS |

sections.heading: Port types
bullets: Access port: belongs to one VLAN and sends/receives untagged frames; for end hosts.
Trunk port: carries many VLANs with tags; between switches, or to routers and servers.
Native VLAN: frames on a trunk without a tag are assigned to it; both ends must agree.

sections.heading: Inter-VLAN routing
sections.body: Hosts in different VLANs are in different subnets, so traffic must be routed. Options: router-on-a-stick (a trunk to a router with a subinterface per VLAN), or a Layer 3 switch with switched virtual interfaces (SVIs).

sections.code:
vlan 10

interface Gi0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
interface Gi0/24
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 switchport trunk native vlan 99

bullets: Switch spoofing: an attacker negotiates a trunk via DTP. Disable with `switchport nonegotiate` and set ports to access.
Double tagging: an outer native-VLAN tag is stripped by the first switch, exposing the inner tag. Use an unused native VLAN and tag it, and never put users on it.

sections.body: Service providers stack an outer S-tag (TPID 0x88a8) on a customer's C-tag so customer VLANs stay private across the provider network.
IP phones are often placed in a separate voice VLAN, and PCP bits mark voice for priority queuing.

bullets: No connectivity across a trunk: VLAN not allowed or not created on the far switch.
Host in the wrong VLAN or wrong subnet/gateway.
Commands: show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk.

takeaways: 802.1Q adds a 4-byte tag with a 12-bit VLAN ID (1-4094).
Access ports are untagged for one VLAN; trunks carry many VLANs tagged.
Different VLANs need a router or Layer 3 switch to talk.
Harden against switch spoofing and double tagging.
